theme: The northern campaign; the defeated kings
readingInstruction: Read Joshua 11:1-12:24. Chapter 11 tells of the northern campaign and the summary of Joshua’s victories. Chapter 12 is a list of defeated kings, which may seem dry. Read it as a record of God’s faithfulness. Pay attention to the repeated phrase “as the LORD had commanded Moses.”
settingTheScene: The southern campaign is complete. Now, in the north, a larger coalition gathers under Jabin, king of Hazor, with a massive army, “as many as the sand on the seashore,” along with horses and chariots. For Israelite infantry, chariots were the most terrifying weapon of the age. The odds look impossible. Yet God speaks to Joshua with the same words he has used before: “Do not be afraid of them.” The chapter then steps back and offers a summary of the war and a list of the kings defeated on both sides of the Jordan. It reads like a ledger, and in a sense it is: a record of what God did in fulfillment of what he promised.
observation: Jabin of Hazor gathers a coalition of northern kings with a huge army, horses, and chariots (11:1-5).
The LORD tells Joshua, “Do not be afraid of them, for tomorrow at this time I will give over all of them” (11:6).
Joshua is told to hamstring the horses and burn the chariots with fire (11:6, 9).
Hazor, “formerly the head of all those kingdoms,” is burned (11:10-11).
“Joshua did to them just as the LORD said to him” (11:9), and “as the LORD had commanded Moses his servant, so Moses commanded Joshua” (11:15).
“There was not a city that made peace with the people of Israel except the Hivites of Gibeon” (11:19).
“It was the LORD’s doing to harden their hearts that they should come against Israel in battle” (11:20).
Chapter 12 lists thirty-one defeated kings, beginning with the two east of the Jordan, Sihon and Og (12:1-24).
interpretation:
The northern campaign shows the pattern of the conquest in miniature: a threat that looks impossible, a word from God, and a victory that comes through obedience. The command to hamstring the horses and burn the chariots is a notable detail. God is teaching Israel not to depend on the military technology of the nations. Psalm 20:7 will later put it this way: “Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we trust in the name of the LORD our God.” The order is a test of dependence. If Israel keeps the horses, they might start to trust them.

The chapter also reveals something about the nature of the conquest. Verse 20 says it was “the LORD’s doing to harden their hearts.” This is the same language used of Pharaoh. The nations of Canaan were not innocent bystanders who were randomly attacked. They were in rebellion, and the war was an act of judgment. God allowed their resistance to run its course. Many readers struggle with this, and the Bible doesn’t hide it. But Scripture is consistent in how it frames the matter: God judges sin, and he does so with justice. Paul takes up the same theme in Romans 9-11, where hardening and mercy sit together in God’s plan.

The repeated phrase “as the LORD commanded Moses” also deserves attention. Joshua is not an innovator. He is a faithful follower of the word of God. The victories happen because he carries out what has been commanded. The author makes it a refrain, because he wants the reader to see that Israel’s success depends not on military genius but on obedience to a word.

Chapter 12 closes the first half of the book with a list. At first it seems like a dry ledger, but it carries a quiet testimony. God remembers each defeated king. The record is a monument. It tells every generation of Israel that these were real enemies, defeated at real places, by real power. When the people doubt, they can look at the list. The God who did all this will not abandon them. And Christians read the list with a larger horizon. The enemies Christ has defeated are far greater: sin, death, and the devil. The cross and resurrection are the real Jericho, and the church is called to live in light of a victory that is already won.
connection: The “hardening” language connects to Exodus 4-14 and to Romans 9:17-18. Trust in horses versus the name of the LORD appears in Psalm 20:7, 33:16-17, and Isaiah 31:1. The commands to Moses are in Deuteronomy 7 and 20. Sihon and Og were defeated in Numbers 21, which you read earlier. The theme of enemy kings defeated looks forward to Colossians 2:15, where Christ “disarmed the rulers and authorities.”
application:
First, ask what your chariots are. What do you rely on that is not God: a plan, a savings account, a network of influence? None of these are evil in themselves, but they may be places where trust has quietly moved. Ask the Lord what to release.

Second, make obedience a habit. Joshua succeeded because he did what he was told, even when it did not make military sense. Choose one clear command of Scripture that you have been delaying, and do it this week.

Third, keep a record. Write down a short list of the ways God has defeated something in your life: a habit, a fear, a broken relationship. Read it when you are discouraged.

Fourth, remember that Christ has won the decisive battle. Live from his victory, not toward it.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to keep you from trusting in chariots and horses, whatever those are in your life.
Ask him to teach you to obey even when his word seems strange.
Thank Christ for disarming the powers that oppose you.
